report.source_text: One week after her initial presentation, she returned to the pediatrician's office with worsening symptoms. Though she had been taking amoxicillin-clavulanate as directed, the swelling on her right neck increased and began to have erythema and tenderness. She did not have fevers and was otherwise at baseline activity. Upon physical exam, she was noted to have right anterior superior cervical lymphadenopathy with overlying erythema. There was concern for inadequate antibiotic coverage or an underlying abscess. Amoxicillin-clavulanate was stopped, and she was switched to clindamycin to cover for possible community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. An ultrasound was ordered to further evaluate for a parotid abscess.

clinician.final_diagnosis: the parotid abscess in this patient is determined to be idiopathic in nature
clinician.trajectory_summary: A four-year-old female presented with a right neck lump, initially diagnosed as lymphadenitis and treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate. Despite initial subjective improvement, symptoms worsened after one week, leading to a change in antibiotics to clindamycin and concern for an abscess. An ultrasound identified a collection in the right submandibular region, and a subsequent CT scan confirmed an isolated parotid gland abscess, ruling out ductal disease, stones, or anatomical variations. The patient underwent incision and drainage of the abscess. Gram stain, fungal cultures, and acid-fast bacilli cultures of the drained purulent fluid were all negative, leading to the conclusion of an idiopathic parotid abscess.

Symptoms worsened after one week despite antibiotic treatment, with increased swelling, erythema, and tenderness, leading to a change in antibiotics and concern for an abscess.
Ultrasound identified a 2.2x2.0x1.5 cm collection in the right submandibular region, determined to be an abscess.
CT scan confirmed a right neck infection confined to the parotid gland, identified as an isolated parotid gland abscess.
CT scan showed no evidence of ductal disease, stones, or anatomical variations in the parotid gland.
Incision and drainage of the abscess were performed, yielding purulent fluid.
Gram stain, fungal cultures, and acid-fast bacilli cultures of the drained fluid returned negative.
